content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper studies the drawbacks of both constrained score-based models (CSBM) and unconstrained score-based models (USBM). 

As for USBM, the paper constructs a particular case where a USBM and a ground-truth score function are very close regarding the score-matching loss while USBM is inefficient for sampling. 

As for CSBM, the paper argues that CSBM is limited because of the restricted architecture. Such an argument has been investigated in prior work (Salimans & Ho, 2021). 

The paper attempts to relieve the problem by training a USBM with a regularization term that encourages it to be conservative. The regularization is directly inspired by the prior work (Glotzl & Richters, 2020). Using the Hutchinson trace estimator, the paper develops an efficient algorithm to estimate the regularization.

The paper evaluates all methods on toy datasets and 4 image datasets of size 32x32 in terms of FID, precision, and recall. The proposed method outperforms CSBM and USBM marginally.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength.
1. The paper is clearly written and well organized.


Weakness.
1. The paper constructs a very particular case in Sec. 3.1 to motivate the proposed method. It is oversimplified and significantly weakens the motivation of the paper in my opinion. 

1.1 It does not consider the optimization of score models. It only proves that a terrible model exists while it is unclear how likely USBM will converge to such a terrible model after training. 

1.2 It does not consider the inductive bias of neural networks. The USBM is not optimized in the function space but in a family of neural networks with convolution and pooling for image modeling. Is it possible that such a terrible model will be eliminated by such inductive bias?

1.3 It is a toy example in 2D space. How do things change in a high-dimensional space?

2. The experiments are not convincing enough

2.1 The improvements of the proposed method are very marginal and the data are of size 32x32, which is clearly far from the SOTA SBMs. Considering the additional complexity of estimating the regularization and the missing theoretical analysis, the significance of the paper is limited. 

2.2 The evaluation can be improved as well. First, Section 3.1 claims that the proposed method is suitable with limited time steps will I did not see an experiment with fewer inference time steps. Second, it considers the VE process only while VP is more popular in SBMs. Finally, sometimes FID is misleading, it is better to present likelihood results as well as human evaluation results.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarify: very clear. 

Quality: limited significance. See the weakness above.

Novelty: the regularization form and the drawback of CSBM have been investigated in previous work. The drawback of USBM is novel for me. 

Reproducibility: reproducible.

content.title: Response to Reviewer YXv3 (Part 2/2)
content.comment:
**Weakness B.** The experiments are not convincing enough
- 2.1 The improvements of the proposed method are very marginal and the data are of size 32x32, which is clearly far from the SOTA SBMs. Considering the additional complexity of estimating the regularization and the missing theoretical analysis, the significance of the paper is limited.
- 2.2 The evaluation can be improved as well. First, Section 3.1 claims that the proposed method is suitable with limited time steps will I did not see an experiment with fewer inference time steps. Second, it considers the VE process only while VP is more popular in SBMs. Finally, sometimes FID is misleading, it is better to present likelihood results as well as human evaluation results.

**Response.** With regard to the reviewer’s comment 2.1, we would like to point out that the primary purpose of this paper is to highlight the importance of preserving both the architectural flexibility as well as the property of conservativeness, and to derive a regularization loss that can be scaled to high-dimensional space.  To meet this objective, we utilized four sets of experiments and a theoretical analysis throughout this paper, which are summarized as follows:
- (E1) Experiment on sampling efficiency in Section 3.1.
- (E2) Experiments on the 8-Gaussian, Checkerboard, and Spirals datasets in Section 3.2,
- (E3) Experiments on the CIFAR-10, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and SVHN datasets in Section 5.
- (E4) Experiments on one-layered auto-encoder in Section 6.
- (A1) Theoretical analysis on the time complexity of $\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{QC}^{\mathrm{tr}}$ in Sections 4.1 and 4.2.

In the first set of experiments (E1), we are able to demonstrate that the non-conservativeness of an SGM can lead to a degraded sampling efficiency even in a low-dimensional example. In the second set of experiments (E2), we examine the impacts of the architectural flexibility of an SGM on its modeling ability and sampling performance using three two-dimensional datasets.  In the third set of experiments (E3), we validated the effectiveness of the regularizer on four image-based datasets. Furthermore, we performed the fourth set of experiments (E4) using a one-layered autoencoder to demonstrate the advantage of QCSGMs over CSGMs. Apart from the above empirical evidence, we provide a theoretical analysis of the computational time complexity of $\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{QC}^{\mathrm{tr}}$ to showcase the scalability of the proposed regularization loss on high-dimensional cases in (A1). 

With regard to comment 2.2, we modified Section 3.1 to include the number of function evaluations (NFE) as the metric for evaluating the sampling efficiency. The results in terms of NFE as well as the sampling performance (i.e., FID, IS, Precision, and Recall) reported in Tables 3 and 4 demonstrate that the proposed method is able to outperform the baseline methods. 

Moreover, in the updated version, we included an additional comparison between QC-NCSN++ and the baseline methods on the Negative Log Likelihood (i.e., NLL) metric in Table 5. The results also suggest that the proposed method is able to achieve superior results on the NLL metric to the baseline methods. 

Finally, the diffusion processes (i.e., VE and VP) are not the focus of this paper, since the proposed method does not modify the sampling algorithm. In this paper, we adopt VE as our diffusion process as many famous prior works [3,5,6,7,8]. 

[1] Diffusion Models Beat GANs on Image Synthesis, Prafulla Dhariwal et al., NeurIPS 2021. (url: https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06991) \
[2] Maximum Likelihood Training of Score-Based Diffusion Models, Yang Song et al., NeurIPS 2021. (url: https://openreview.net/pdf?id=AklttWFnxS9) \
[3] Maximum Likelihood Training for Score-Based Diffusion ODEs by High-Order Denoising Score Matching, Cheng Lu et al., ICML 2022. (url: https://proceedings.mlr.press/v162/lu22f/lu22f.pdf) \
[4] Diffusion Normalizing Flow, Qinsheng Zhang et al., NeurIPS 2021. (url: https://openreview.net/forum?id=x1Lp2bOlVIo) \
[5] Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution, Yang Song et al., NeurIPS 2019. (url: https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.05600) \
[6] Improved Techniques for Training Score-Based Generative Models, Yang Song et al., NeurIPS 2020. (url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.09011) \
[7] Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations, Yang Song et al., ICLR 2021. (url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.13456) \
[8] Efficient Learning of Generative Models via Finite-Difference Score Matching, Tianyu Pang et al., NeurIPS 2020. (url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.03317)

content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the time and effort spent on the reviews. We have modified the paper and summarized the updates in the `Summary of Revision’ comment above. The followings are our responses to the reviewer’s questions:

---

**Weakness A.** The paper constructs a very particular case in Sec. 3.1 to motivate the proposed method. It is oversimplified and significantly weakens the motivation of the paper in my opinion. 
- 1.1 It does not consider the optimization of score models. It only proves that a terrible model exists while it is unclear how likely USBM will converge to such a terrible model after training.
- 1.2 It does not consider the inductive bias of neural networks. The USBM is not optimized in the function space but in a family of neural networks with convolution and pooling for image modeling. Is it possible that such a terrible model will be eliminated by such inductive bias?
- 1.3 It is a toy example in 2D space. How do things change in a high-dimensional space?

**Response.** We would like to clarify that Section 3.1 is introduced for an illustrative purpose, and it is indeed a special case that does not involve the optimization process as well as the inductive bias of neural networks. Such an experimental setup, however, allows us to control the approximation errors of an SGM and compare the influence of its non-conservativeness on the sampling process. To avoid confusion, we modified the wording in Section 3.1, and highlighted the revised parts in red.

As for the comments 1.1 to 1.3, our experimental results presented in Section 3.2 and Section 5 involve the optimization process (comment 1.1). In addition, our model (i.e., QC-NCSN++) presented in Section 5 is trained on high-dimensional datasets (comment 1.3), and takes the inductive bias of neural networks (comment 1.2) into account.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors introduce quasi-conservative score-based generative models (QCSGMs). Starting from the categorization of score-based generative models (SGMs) in constrained SGMs (CSGMs) and unconstrained (USGMs), they introduce the property conservativeness, meaning that the score function has zero rotation, which is satisfied by CSGMs, but not USGMs. Using a simple example, they try to demonstrate why the lack of conservativeness can reduce the sampling efficiency. Since CSGMs are less expressive, they show how USGMs can be regularized to be "more conservative", i.e. have a smaller rotation. They achieve this by including a regularization term forcing the Jacobian of the score function to be more symmetric.
They apply their method to a toy dataset and several image datasets, and their method performs slightly better that the unregularized procedures.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths

The paper has a clear structure, building up in explaining the background and categorization of SGMs and explaining their respective merits and shortcomings. To the best of my knowledge, the conservativeness has not been investigated for SGMs so far, so their considerations are valuable to get a better understanding of how SGMs behave. The idea of regularizing USGMs is simple and novel.

### Weaknesses

Adding the regularization loss including the Jacobian of the score function adds a significant computational overhead to training. I acknowledge the author's effort to make the computation as efficient as possible, but there should be a runtime comparison. One argument the author's make for QCSGMs is sample efficiency. However, as far as I can see, they did not investigate the sampling efficiency of their model on the toy setup where non-conservative USGMs fail. Moreover, the improvement of QSGMs over USGMs is very small, even regarding the sampling efficiency. Since the author's did not do multiple runs of their experiments on the image datasets, it is not clear whether there is an improvement beyond the standard error.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written and the main ideas presented in the paper are novel. They describe their implementation in detail. However, the improvement of QCSGMs over USGMs are marginal and it is not clear whether they are significant.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Due to the lack of evidence whether the method is significantly better than the baseline on real-world datasets and the missing discussion of the computational overhead, I tend towards rejecting this paper. However, I am open for a discussion with the authors and the other reviewers.

Edit after rebuttal:

I appreciate the author's effort to improve their manuscript. However, I share skepticism of the other reviewers about the work and, hence, will not change my score.

We thank the reviewer for the time and effort spent on the reviews. We have modified the paper and summarized the updates in the 'Summary of Revision' comment above. The followings are our responses to the reviewer’s questions:

---

**Weakness A.** Adding the regularization loss including the Jacobian of the score function adds a significant computational overhead to training. I acknowledge the author's effort to make the computation as efficient as possible, but there should be a runtime comparison. 

**Response.** With regard to the reviewer’s question about the learning speed, we have added a discussion on the training time of QC-NCSN++ in Section A.6.2, and presented a runtime comparison in Table A5.

---

**Weakness B.** One argument the author's make for QCSGMs is sample efficiency. However, as far as I can see, they did not investigate the sampling efficiency of their model on the toy setup where non-conservative USGMs fail. 

**Response.** We modified Section 3.1 to include a comparison of the original vector field (with a high Asym) with another vector field (with a zero Asym) under the same estimation error.

---

**Weakness C** Moreover, the improvement of QSGMs over USGMs is very small, even regarding the sampling efficiency. Since the author's did not do multiple runs of their experiments on the image datasets, it is not clear whether there is an improvement beyond the standard error.

**Response.** We have included new experimental results on the real-world datasets in Tables 3-5. They demonstrate noticeable improvements in terms of both sampling efficiency and performance. 

With regard to the reviewer's question about the variances of the results, we evaluated the confidence intervals of the experimental results on the real-world datasets and presented them in Table A4 in the updated version.

As for the reviewer’s comment on the performance improvement, we briefly compare our NLL improvements in Table 5 (i.e., **0.08** on CIFAR-10, **0.13** on ImageNet, **0.14** on SVHN, and **0.06** on CIFAR-100) to the improvements in several other papers.

- [1] proposed an architecture that improves NLL $\leq$ **0.05** on both CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.
- [2] proposed a LW method that improves NLL $\leq$ **0.10** on CIFAR-10, but $\leq$ **0.02** on ImageNet.
- [3] improved over baseline with a margin **0.03** on the NLL metric on the CIFAR-10 dataset.

In conclusion, the performance benefits of QC-NCSN++ are in fact substantial from the perspective of the previous research endeavors.

[1] Emerging Convolutions for Generative Normalizing Flows, Emiel Hoogeboom et al., ICML 2019. (url: https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.11137) \
[2] Maximum Likelihood Training of Score-Based Diffusion Models, Yang Song et al., NeurIPS 2021. (url: https://openreview.net/pdf?id=AklttWFnxS9) \
[3] Neural Spline Flows, Conor Durkan et al., NeurIPS 2019. (url: https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.04032)

---

Overall, we would like to thank the reviewer again for the constructive advice.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper considers preserving the conservativeness of learned score field while retaining architectural flexibility at the same time. Previous work either constraining the model architecture to strictly enforce conservativeness (CSGM), or completely ignore the conservativeness (USGM). To combine the best of two worlds, the paper apply a symmetric Jacobian constraint as the soft conservativeness regularizer. They further circumvent the computation of Jocabian matrix by Huchison trace estimator. Experimentally, the proposed method promotes the conservativeness of the learned score function and improve the sample quality on several image datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strong points

- The paper proposed a new regularizer for controlling the conservativeness of score-based models. The regularizer quantifies the non-conservativeness by the Frobenius norm for the rotational density.

- The paper utilizes the Hutchinson trace estimator to obtain a practical version of the regularizer.

- Experimentally, the proposed method improves score-based model VE on image generation tasks, in terms of image quality and conservativeness. 

### Weak points

- The toy experiments in Sec 3.1 do not showcase the effectiveness of conservativeness. The large number of sampling steps could be caused by high estimation error rather than high Asym/NAsym. A more fair setup is to compare low Asym/high estimation error with high Asym/low estimation error. 

- The biggest concern I have is the practical utility of the conservativeness of generative models. The performance of generative models is typically measured in two aspects: generation quality (e.g. FID scores) and sampling speed (e.g. NFEs). According to Table 3, the proposed QC-NCSN++ has worse-off sample quality on standard benchmarks such as CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32x32, as measured by FID (FID is observed to be more stable than IS, and better capture the sample diversity). In addition, the comparisons of Asym and NAsym do not convey useful information, as QC explicitly minimizes these quantities. The advantage of a "more conservative" score function in practice remains unclear. The experiments seem to suggest that the QC regularizer harms the performance of modern convolutional networks.

- (Continuing on point above) A main motivation for the QC regularizer is that it allows for explicitly controlling the trade-off between expressiveness and conservativeness. Could the author provide some experimental results if we varied the balance factor $\lambda$? How did the author select the current hyper-parameter $\lambda$?


- Could the authors report results on higher resolution datasets, such as ImageNet 64x64, in the future? I understand it could be hard to finish the experiment in a short rebuttal period, but it would be really helpful to see whether conservativeness brings more performance gain in higher dimensional datasets. Another possibility is to apply QC onto other advanced generative models requiring conservativeness, such as Poisson Flow Generative Models.

- The training of QCSGM requires two extra back-propagation through the neural network, resulting in longer training time. Could the authors discuss the training overhead in more detail? It would be helpful to visualize the wall-clock training time versus FID scores for baselines and QC.

 
### Writing suggestions:

- "Cifar" -> "CIFAR". The latter is more commonly used by the community.

- The derivation of the actual training process takes too much space in the main text. The core idea is clear and neat. The detailed practical implementation could be deferred to the Appendix.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is generally well-written. The explicit control over conservativeness and expressiveness is novel and interesting. However, the benefit of a more conservative score function is unclear in practice and in theory when sacrificing expressiveness. The proposed regularizer for conservativeness also incurs additional training overhead.
content.summary_of_the_review: The reviewer is leaning toward rejecting the current version, because the practical and theoretical value of incorporating a more conservative score function while sacrificing expressiveness is unclear.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

**Response.**  We included new experimental results in Tables 3-5 to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Table 3 reports the sampling performance of QC-NCSN++ with an ODE sampler. The results show that QC-NCSN++ is able to outperform the baselines in terms of both FID and NFE. On the other hand, Table 4 reports the sampling performance of QC-NCSN++ with a PC sampler. The results also reveal that QC-NCSN++ is able to outperform the baselines in terms of FID under a smaller value of NFE. Furthermore, we included a comparison of U-NCSN++, C-NCSN++, and QC-NCSN++ in terms of a likelihood-based metric (i.e., NLL) in Table 5. I understand it could be hard to finish the experiment in a short rebuttal period, but it would be really helpful to see whether conservativeness brings more performance gain in higher dimensional datasets. content.comment:
I would like to thank the authors for their efforts in improving the manuscripts, e.g., more fair comparison in the toy example and the condensation of the main text.

However, the current experimental results are still conducted in an unrepresentative way, and cannot showcase the effectiveness of the proposed method. Current Table 3/Table 4 show that QC-NCSN++ can improve VE-ODE/VE-SDE with smaller NFEs. Both settings are not widely used in practice. I would suggest applying QC to the more popular VP [1] or EDM [2] as the baselines for ODE solvers (as also pointed out by Reviewer YXv3), or to other ODE frameworks like PFGM [3]. In addition, it's uncommon to decrease the NFE when using PC sampler, unless explicitly integrating Wiener process in the larger time intervals. 

A minor comment for another modification: the authors report the training time versus FID scores in Table A.6. It's unclear whether the QC-NCSN++ can indeed achieve a higher FID score than the U-NCSN++ given the same training time in the one-shot comparison. I suggest plotting the whole training dynamics across different checkpoints (FID versus training time), to provide better support for the argument.

I will keep my score unchanged due to the incompleteness of the experiments stated above.

[2] Karras et al., Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Generative Models, 2022.

[3] Xu et al., Poisson Flow Generative Models, 2022.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents a method of encouraging the score-based generative models to model a conservative vector field. Traditionally, these models are interpreted as learning the gradient of the target distribution's log-probability function. This is the gradient of a scalar function so the true value has a property known as being conservative. This means the gradient field has 0 curl. Typically gradient in a score based model is parameterized with an unconstrained neural network which has no guarantees to have this property. 

This paper proposes to regularize the network used in a score-based generative model to be conservative (instead of explicitly forcing it to have this property). This is done by encouraging JtJ to be small. Hutchinson's trace estimator is used to produce unbiased estimates of the regularizers value which are sufficient for training. 

The authors provide some theory on cases where the score estimation error can be arbitrarily small but the sampling efficiency can be considerably hindered by the lack of conservativeness. 

The authors present empirical results on a set of benchmark datasets where their conservation regularizer improves sampling quality.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

The paper is clearly written and the motivation is well described. The proposed approach is simple and easy to implement. 


Weaknesses:

While I liked the paper, I feel like the introduction and related work sections were a bit long. I do not think the section on Metropolis-Hastings was necessary since it is not utilized in the work. I feel like a lot of this could be kicked to the appendix or replaced with references to related work. 

I found section 3.1 somewhat hard to understand. I get the premise of the section. You want to show that even when the loss function is small, sampling can still be inefficient due to lack of conservativity. It seems that the main metric used here was the precision recall metric. I was not familiar with the precision recall metric for evaluating generative models. I had to read a referenced paper to understand it. I think it should be briefly mentioned in the related work if this is the main metric used to justify the method. 

As well, I found the empirical results somewhat uncompelling. The difference between the quasi conservative methods and the unconservative methods seems small. I would be more convinced by a likelihood based evaluation (from RAISE or AIS). Also, why was the conservative (s(x) = ||x - f(x)||^2) score model not presented in this section? That seemed to perform well in the toy results section, so I'd expect a comparison here. 

Last, it seems that this method requires a fair bit more compute than the unconservative score model. Is this then a fair comparison if we are comparing two models which have drastically different learning speeds and memory requirements? I think a more fair comparison would be to increase the size of the unconservative model to match the compute of the quasi-conservative model.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing is clear and the method is well-explained. The approach is interesting and this addresses an issue with these models that has been discussed for some time now. The novelty is moderate as I have not seen hutchinson's estimator applied to this specific application (encouraging conservativity) but I have seen the same estimator used before (for example, to regularize the path length of neural ODEs). The results seem reproducible. The authors clearly state their experimental details and list all hyper-parameters used.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents a method for encouraging score-based generative models to fit a conservative vector field like their true target. The method is based on hutchinson's trace estimator. The method clearly encourages learned models to be more conservative than un-regularized models but the impact on scalable model performance is not particularly clear and the benchmarks and empirical results are somewhat lacking.

content.title: Response to Reviewer xCU1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the time and effort spent on the reviews. We have modified the paper and summarized the updates in the 'Summary of Revision' comment above. The followings are our responses to the reviewer’s questions:

---

**Weakness A.** While I liked the paper, I feel like the introduction and related work sections were a bit long. I do not think the section on Metropolis-Hastings was necessary since it is not utilized in the work. I feel like a lot of this could be kicked to the appendix or replaced with references to related work. 

**Response.** We thank the reviewer for the suggestion and have removed the paragraph describing Metropolis-Hastings in Section 2.

---

**Weakness B.** I found section 3.1 somewhat hard to understand. I get the premise of the section. You want to show that even when the loss function is small, sampling can still be inefficient due to lack of conservativity. It seems that the main metric used here was the precision recall metric. I was not familiar with the precision recall metric for evaluating generative models. I had to read a referenced paper to understand it. I think it should be briefly mentioned in the related work if this is the main metric used to justify the method.

**Response.** We have included the descriptions of the Precision and Recall metrics in Section 3.2 as suggested by the reviewer.

---

**Weakness C.** As well, I found the empirical results somewhat uncompelling. The difference between the quasi conservative methods and the unconservative methods seems small. I would be more convinced by a likelihood based evaluation (from RAISE or AIS). Also, why was the conservative (s(x) = ||x - f(x)||^2) score model not presented in this section? That seemed to perform well in the toy results section, so I'd expect a comparison here.

**Response.** RAISE and AIS are not applicable to non-conservative score models, since their evaluation procedures require an energy function to be available. Nevertheless, we evaluated the performance of the proposed method and that of the baselines on an additional likelihood-based metric (i.e., NLL), and presented the results in Table 5. It is observed that QC-NCSN++ outperforms the baselines in terms of NLL across all of the real-world datasets presented in Section 5 (i.e., CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, ImageNet 32x32). As for the evaluation results of the conservative score models, we report them in Tables 3 and 5.

---

**Weakness D.** Last, it seems that this method requires a fair bit more compute than the unconservative score model. Is this then a fair comparison if we are comparing two models which have drastically different learning speeds and memory requirements? I think a more fair comparison would be to increase the size of the unconservative model to match the compute of the quasi-conservative model.

**Response.** With regard to the learning speed, we believe that the comparison is fair since the performance of NCSN++ does not improve even when it is trained for an extended period of time. The results are added to the Appendix A6.2 (Table A4).

It would be unfair if the model size of the unconservative model is increased just for aligning the memory usage with the proposed method, as both of them are implemented based on exactly the same model architecture. The main memory and computation overhead of the proposed method stems from the additional backpropagation pass instead of extra model parameters. As a result, we consider that the comparison presented in the manuscript is appropriate.

---

Overall, we would like to thank the reviewer again for the constructive advice.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer xCU1

content.title: Thank you
content.comment:
I thank the authors for making the changes they did to address my concerns. I think they improve the paper and make it more clear to the less-informed reader. Having said that I disagree with some elements of the authors' response. You can utilize AIS to evaluate non-conservative models. You can utilize an unadjusted langevin transition such as [1]. You can also utilize the elbo as in [2] to obtain a lower-bound on likelihood which would be very useful to understand the quality of the various models. 

I also disagree with the authors' statement that it would be unfair to compare with a model which equalizes time and memory usage to the quasi-conservative approach. If you propose a new technique that utilizes the same model but can only be trained w/ 10x memory, then this means at the large scale we can only use a model 1/10th the size (approximately) which may greatly degrade quality for larger-scale models. As we have learned in recent years, simply scaling up models can lead to large gains in performance so it is valuable to give the reader some context on what could be achieved by matching the compute requirements of the baseline approach. 

While I am generally optimistic about these ideas, I feel more context is needed to fully understand the method and it appears that the current improvement is not particularly large. For these reasons I will keep my score the same.  


[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.06707
[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239

content.title: Summary of Revision
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their constructive comments and suggestions. We have made a number of modifications to our paper and highlighted the revised parts in red in the updated manuscript. The overall modifications are summarized as follows:

---

**Main manuscript**

**[Section 2.2]**
- Removed the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm throughout the paper. `(Reviewer xCU1: Weakness A)`
- Added descriptions of the time-inhomogeneous sampling process based on an SDE.

**[Section 3.1]**
- Clarified the purpose of the experiment presented in Section 3.1, and modified the wording. `(Reviewer YXv3: Weakness A)`
- Added a conservative vector field ($s_C$) for a comparison purpose. `(Reviewer TYb7: Weakness A)`
- Added "number of function evaluations (NFE)" as an evaluation metric in Fig. 1. The results reveal that $s_C$ can outperform $s_U$ in terms of NFE under the same approximation error. We conclude that the non-conservativeness may decelerate the sampling process. `(Reviewer TYb7: Weakness B)`; `(Reviewer 2fxK: Weakness B)`; `(Reviewer YXv3: Weakness B)`

**[Section 3.2]**
- Included descriptions of NLL, Precision, and Recall. `(Reviewer xCU1: Weakness B)`
- Added the NLL metric in Table 1, which reveals that QCSGM outperforms the baseline in terms of score errors, NLL, Precision, and Recall, across the three toy datasets. `(Reviewer xCU1: Weakness C)`

**[Section 4.2]**
- Condensed the paragraph, and moved the details to the appendix (Section 4.2.3). `(Reviewer TYb7: Weakness G)`

**[Section 5]**
- Changed the non-conservative baseline notation from 'NCSN++' to 'U-NCSN++', and added a conservative baseline: 'C-NCSN++'. `(Reviewer xCU1: Weakness C)`
- Moved the results in the original Table 3 to the `NFE=2,000’ row of Table 4 and Table A8 in the appendix.
- Added more experimental results to Table 3-5.
  - Evaluated the sampling performance using an ODE sampler in the new Table 3. `(Reviewer TYb7: Weakness B)`; `(Reviewer 2fxK: Weakness C)`
    - The results show that QC-NCSN++ outperforms the baselines in terms of NFE, FID, IS, Precision, and Recall.
  - Reported the sampling performance with a PC sampler in Table 4. `(Reviewer TYb7: Weakness B)`; `(Reviewer 2fxK: Weakness C)`
    - The results reveal that QC-NCSN++ is able to outperform the baselines in terms of FID, IS, Precision, and Recall under a smaller value of NFE. 
    - The results also demonstrate that QC-NCSN++ performs on par with the baselines, with slightly better IS, Precision, Recall, and slightly inferior FID under a larger value of  NFE.
  - Included likelihood-based evaluation (i.e., NLL) in Table 5. `(Reviewer xCU1: Weakness C)`; `(Reviewer TYb7: Weakness B)`; `(Reviewer 2fxK: Weakness C)`
    - The results reveal that QC-NCSN++ outperforms the baselines in terms of NLL across all of the four real-world datasets.

---

**Appendix**
- Included the confidence interval of the real-world experiments in Table A4. `(Reviewer xCU1: Weakness D)`
- Included a comparison of the time and memory consumption in Table A5. `(Reviewer xCU1: Weakness D)`; `(Reviewer 2fxK: Weakness A)`
- Included the sampling performance of U-NCSN++ trained with an extended period in Table A6. `(Reviewer TYb7: Weakness E)`
- Included a performance comparison of QC-NCSN++ trained with different $\lambda$ values in Table A7. `(Reviewer TYb7: Weakness C)`

---

**A minor issue throughout the paper**
- Modified 'Cifar' to 'CIFAR'. `(Reviewer TYb7: Weakness F)`
